frontHtml: Localise facial weakness that spares the forehead to the contralateral upper motor neuron pathway.
backHtml: a spared forehead means a central lesion on the side opposite the facial droop.

frontHtml: Treat typical Bell palsy with an early oral corticosteroid and eye protection, without routine testing.
backHtml: typical Bell palsy needs a steroid within 72 hours and eye protection; it does not need tests.

frontHtml: Identify group B streptococcus as the cause of neonatal meningitis from host age and Gram stain.
backHtml: gram-positive cocci in chains in neonatal CSF mean group B streptococcus.

frontHtml: Link meningococcal septic shock and DIC to lipooligosaccharide endotoxin.
backHtml: meningococcal shock and DIC are driven by endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide).

frontHtml: Describe the activation and mechanism of acyclovir in HSV encephalitis.
backHtml: acyclovir needs viral thymidine kinase; resistance comes from thymidine kinase mutations.

frontHtml: Explain the pathogenesis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
backHtml: prion disease is self-propagating misfolding of PrP into a β-sheet form, with spongiform change and no inflammation.

frontHtml: Identify Cryptococcus neoformans from its morphology in an HIV-associated meningitis.
backHtml: India ink-positive meningitis with high opening pressure in advanced HIV is Cryptococcus, an encapsulated yeast.

frontHtml: Identify oligodendrocytes as the target cell in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
backHtml: PML is JC virus destruction of oligodendrocytes, a known risk of natalizumab.

frontHtml: Localise the lesion of tabes dorsalis to the dorsal roots and dorsal columns.
backHtml: tabes dorsalis destroys dorsal roots and columns: sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, areflexia, Argyll Robertson pupils.

frontHtml: Predict the organisms of a brain abscess from its source of spread.
backHtml: brain abscess from a sinus or tooth: viridans streptococci (S. anginosus group) and anaerobes.

frontHtml: Sequence blood cultures, dexamethasone, empirical antibiotics and imaging in suspected bacterial meningitis.
backHtml: if CT must come before LP, give cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics first.

frontHtml: Recommend chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis.
backHtml: close contacts of meningococcal disease get chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin, rifampin or ceftriaxone) without waiting.

frontHtml: Interpret a cerebrospinal fluid profile to diagnose tuberculous meningitis.
backHtml: lymphocytic CSF with very high protein and low glucose over weeks suggests tuberculous meningitis.

frontHtml: Start empirical intravenous acyclovir in suspected HSV encephalitis.
backHtml: suspected encephalitis means intravenous acyclovir now, before the PCR result returns.

frontHtml: Choose empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis in an older adult.
backHtml: add ampicillin for Listeria in meningitis over age 50, in pregnancy and with impaired cellular immunity.

frontHtml: Manage cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV, including intracranial pressure and timing of antiretroviral therapy.
backHtml: cryptococcal meningitis: amphotericin plus flucytosine, therapeutic LPs for pressure, and delayed ART.

frontHtml: Treat suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis empirically in advanced HIV.
backHtml: multiple ring lesions with positive Toxoplasma IgG in advanced HIV: treat empirically and re-image.

frontHtml: Treat neurosyphilis with intravenous penicillin G.
backHtml: neurosyphilis needs intravenous penicillin G for 10–14 days; benzathine penicillin is inadequate.

frontHtml: Recognise the CSF findings of multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: CSF-specific oligoclonal IgG bands reflect antibody synthesis inside the CNS in MS.

frontHtml: Localise internuclear ophthalmoplegia to the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
backHtml: INO is named for the side of the eye that fails to adduct, which is the side of the MLF lesion.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism and main risk of natalizumab.
backHtml: natalizumab blocks α4-integrin; screen for JC virus antibodies because of PML risk.

frontHtml: Recognise fingolimod from its mechanism and adverse effects.
backHtml: S1P receptor modulators trap lymphocytes in nodes and can cause first-dose bradycardia.

frontHtml: Associate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with ovarian teratoma.
backHtml: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman: look for an ovarian teratoma.

frontHtml: Distinguish ADEM from multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: ADEM: post-infectious, monophasic, encephalopathy plus multifocal lesions of the same age, usually in a child.

frontHtml: Explain the Uhthoff phenomenon in multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: heat-induced, reversible return of old MS symptoms is conduction block in demyelinated axons, not a relapse.

frontHtml: Order brain MRI after a first episode of optic neuritis.
backHtml: after a first episode of optic neuritis, brain MRI with gadolinium sets MS risk and management.

frontHtml: Distinguish an infection-triggered pseudo-relapse from a true MS relapse.
backHtml: before treating an MS relapse, exclude infection and fever (pseudo-relapse).

frontHtml: Treat an acute disabling relapse of multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: a disabling MS relapse is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone; plasma exchange if refractory.

frontHtml: Investigate for an ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
backHtml: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: image the pelvis for a teratoma and start immunotherapy.

frontHtml: Identify pre-treatment screening required for anti-CD20 therapy in multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: screen for hepatitis B before anti-CD20 therapy.

frontHtml: Manage neurogenic bladder overactivity in multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: MS urgency with a small residual: antimuscarinic or mirabegron; large residual: intermittent catheterisation.

frontHtml: Select disease-modifying therapy for primary progressive multiple sclerosis.
backHtml: ocrelizumab is the agent shown to slow disability in primary progressive MS.

frontHtml: Explain the embryological failure in anencephaly.
backHtml: anencephaly = rostral neuropore failure; raised AFP and polyhydramnios.

frontHtml: Identify folic acid as the nutrient that prevents neural tube defects.
backHtml: periconceptional folic acid prevents most neural tube defects; the dose is higher after an affected pregnancy.

frontHtml: Link holoprosencephaly to the sonic hedgehog pathway.
backHtml: holoprosencephaly reflects defective sonic hedgehog signalling; trisomy 13 is a classic cause.

frontHtml: Localise dissociated sensory loss from a syrinx to the anterior white commissure.
backHtml: a central cord syrinx causes cape-like loss of pain and temperature by cutting crossing fibres in the anterior white commissure.

frontHtml: Describe the molecular function of the tuberous sclerosis gene products.
backHtml: tuberous sclerosis: loss of hamartin/tuberin unleashes mTOR; mTOR inhibitors shrink the tumours.

frontHtml: Identify the function of neurofibromin in neurofibromatosis type 1.
backHtml: NF1 neurofibromin switches off Ras; NF2 merlin is a different, cytoskeletal tumour suppressor.

frontHtml: Explain the molecular basis of von Hippel-Lindau disease.
backHtml: VHL loss stabilises HIF: haemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and polycythaemia.

frontHtml: Explain the leg-predominant pattern of spastic diplegia in preterm infants.
backHtml: preterm periventricular leukomalacia causes spastic diplegia because leg fibres lie nearest the ventricles.

frontHtml: Recommend high-dose periconceptional folic acid after a previous neural tube defect.
backHtml: previous neural tube defect: 4 mg folic acid daily from at least 1 month before conception.

frontHtml: Provide immediate care for a newborn with an open myelomeningocele.
backHtml: newborn myelomeningocele: moist sterile dressing, prone position, latex precautions, closure within 72 hours.

frontHtml: Recognise and evaluate ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction.
backHtml: a child with a shunt and headache, vomiting or drowsiness has shunt failure until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Choose MRI to evaluate a suspected Chiari I malformation with syringomyelia.
backHtml: cough headache with a cape-like sensory loss: MRI the brain and cervical spine for Chiari I and a syrinx.

frontHtml: Treat focal spasticity in a child with cerebral palsy.
backHtml: focal spasticity in cerebral palsy: botulinum toxin plus therapy; tendon surgery only for fixed contracture.

frontHtml: Choose first-line therapy for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex.
backHtml: infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis: vigabatrin first; watch for visual field loss.

frontHtml: Plan surveillance for a child with neurofibromatosis type 1.
backHtml: children with NF1 need yearly eye examinations to detect optic pathway gliomas.

frontHtml: Use magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection in imminent preterm birth.
backHtml: imminent delivery before 32 weeks: give magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection.

frontHtml: Identify the cell of origin of a meningioma from its imaging and histology.
backHtml: meningioma = arachnoid cap cells; whorls and psammoma bodies.

frontHtml: Recognise pilocytic astrocytoma and its favourable prognosis after resection.
backHtml: pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common childhood brain tumour and the most curable by surgery.

frontHtml: Link hemangioblastoma to von Hippel–Lindau disease and the function of the VHL protein.
backHtml: VHL loss stabilises HIF, giving hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma and erythrocytosis.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology of schwannoma in a patient with NF2.
backHtml: bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2; Antoni A/B pattern with Verocay bodies.

frontHtml: Explain hyperprolactinemia from pituitary stalk compression by a nonfunctioning adenoma.
backHtml: mildly raised prolactin with a large sellar mass suggests stalk compression, not a prolactinoma.

frontHtml: Recognise malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma in NF1.
backHtml: rapid growth or new pain in a plexiform neurofibroma means MPNST until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: State the embryologic origin of craniopharyngioma.
backHtml: craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm), the precursor of the anterior pituitary.

frontHtml: Recognise glioblastoma from its imaging and histology.
backHtml: glioblastoma = pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation, often crossing the corpus callosum.

frontHtml: Explain how mutant IDH promotes gliomagenesis through 2-hydroxyglutarate.
backHtml: mutant IDH makes 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits demethylases and causes a hypermethylated, undifferentiated state.

frontHtml: Describe CSF dissemination of medulloblastoma.
backHtml: medulloblastoma spreads through CSF; stage it with spine MRI and CSF cytology.

frontHtml: Recognise ependymoma from its site and perivascular pseudorosettes.
backHtml: perivascular pseudorosettes from the floor of the fourth ventricle = ependymoma.

frontHtml: Associate primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS with Epstein–Barr virus.
backHtml: in advanced HIV, primary CNS lymphoma is EBV-associated; CSF EBV PCR supports it.

frontHtml: Relate temozolomide's alkylating mechanism to MGMT promoter methylation.
backHtml: temozolomide alkylates DNA; MGMT promoter methylation predicts benefit.

frontHtml: Identify the molecular hallmark of diffuse midline glioma of the pons.
backHtml: diffuse midline glioma of the pons is defined by histone H3 K27 alteration.

frontHtml: Apply the molecular criteria for glioblastoma in the WHO CNS5 classification.
backHtml: in adults, IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytoma with TERT, EGFR or +7/−10 is glioblastoma, whatever the histology.

frontHtml: Name lung cancer as the most common source of brain metastases.
backHtml: lung cancer is the leading source of brain metastases.

frontHtml: Explain the gray–white junction location of brain metastases.
backHtml: brain metastases lodge at the gray–white junction because arterioles narrow there.

frontHtml: Recognise melanoma as a source of hemorrhagic brain metastases.
backHtml: hemorrhagic brain metastases suggest melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma or thyroid carcinoma.

frontHtml: Explain vertebral metastasis of prostate cancer through the vertebral venous plexus.
backHtml: prostate cancer spreads to the spine through the valveless vertebral venous plexus and gives sclerotic lesions.

frontHtml: Associate anti-Yo paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with gynecologic and breast cancer.
backHtml: anti-Yo cerebellar degeneration → look for ovarian or breast cancer.

frontHtml: Explain why anti-Hu paraneoplastic syndromes respond poorly to antibody removal.
backHtml: antibodies against intracellular onconeural antigens are markers; T cells cause the damage, and immunotherapy helps little.

frontHtml: Associate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with ovarian teratoma.
backHtml: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman → search for an ovarian teratoma.

frontHtml: Treat a macroprolactinoma with a dopamine agonist first, even with visual field loss.
backHtml: prolactinomas of any size are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

frontHtml: Choose surgery for a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm.
backHtml: a nonfunctioning macroadenoma causing visual loss needs transsphenoidal surgery.

frontHtml: Recognise and treat central diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery.
backHtml: after pituitary surgery, dilute polyuria with high sodium is central diabetes insipidus: give desmopressin.

frontHtml: Give stress-dose glucocorticoid first in pituitary apoplexy.
backHtml: pituitary apoplexy: give IV hydrocortisone first, then consider decompression.

frontHtml: Choose observation with serial imaging for a small, minimally symptomatic vestibular schwannoma.
backHtml: small, minimally symptomatic vestibular schwannomas are watched with serial MRI.

frontHtml: Resect a symptomatic accessible meningioma.
backHtml: symptomatic, accessible meningioma → resect.

frontHtml: Recommend yearly eye examinations for children with NF1.
backHtml: NF1 in childhood: yearly eye examinations to detect optic pathway glioma.

frontHtml: Treat pilocytic astrocytoma with complete surgical resection.
backHtml: pilocytic astrocytoma: complete resection is usually curative.

frontHtml: Choose chemoradiation with temozolomide after resection of glioblastoma.
backHtml: glioblastoma: resection, then radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide.

frontHtml: Biopsy suspected primary CNS lymphoma before giving corticosteroids.
backHtml: suspected primary CNS lymphoma: biopsy before steroids.

frontHtml: Stage medulloblastoma with whole-spine MRI and CSF cytology.
backHtml: stage medulloblastoma with spine MRI and CSF cytology.

frontHtml: Add Pneumocystis prophylaxis for lymphopenia during temozolomide chemoradiation.
backHtml: give Pneumocystis prophylaxis during concurrent temozolomide–radiotherapy.

frontHtml: Image the brain first in a child with signs of a posterior fossa mass.
backHtml: a child with morning headache, ataxia and papilledema needs brain MRI before anything else.

frontHtml: Recognise pseudoprogression after glioblastoma chemoradiation and continue therapy.
backHtml: early post-chemoradiation enhancement in a stable patient: suspect pseudoprogression and keep treating.

frontHtml: Choose levetiracetam for seizures in a patient with a brain tumour.
backHtml: in patients with brain tumours and seizures, prefer a non–enzyme-inducing drug such as levetiracetam.

frontHtml: Manage suspected metastatic spinal cord compression as an emergency.
backHtml: cancer + back pain + neurological deficit: dexamethasone now and emergency whole-spine MRI.

frontHtml: Search for the primary with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis when a brain metastasis is suspected.
backHtml: with a probable brain metastasis and no known cancer, search for the primary with body CT first.

frontHtml: Treat a single accessible symptomatic brain metastasis with resection plus cavity radiosurgery.
backHtml: single accessible symptomatic brain metastasis in a fit patient: resect, then radiosurgery to the cavity.

frontHtml: Choose radiosurgery for a few small brain metastases.
backHtml: a few small brain metastases: radiosurgery, not whole-brain radiotherapy.

frontHtml: Diagnose leptomeningeal metastasis with neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.
backHtml: multilevel cranial and spinal root deficits in cancer: gadolinium MRI of neuraxis, then CSF cytology.

frontHtml: Avoid antiseizure prophylaxis in brain metastases without seizures.
backHtml: no prophylactic antiseizure drugs for brain tumours without seizures.

frontHtml: Search for an ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
backHtml: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: look for and remove an ovarian teratoma, and give immunotherapy.

frontHtml: Choose radiotherapy for cord compression from a radiosensitive tumour in a stable spine.
backHtml: radiosensitive tumour + stable spine: treat cord compression with radiotherapy.

frontHtml: Identify cerebral amyloid angiopathy as the cause of recurrent lobar hemorrhage in older adults.
backHtml: recurrent lobar hemorrhage in an older normotensive patient points to amyloid angiopathy.

frontHtml: Link a pupil-involving oculomotor palsy with sudden headache to a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
backHtml: a third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil and headache means a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Recall the timeline of microscopic changes after a brain infarct.
backHtml: red neurons appear 12–24 hours after ischemic injury.

frontHtml: Explain coma from bilateral damage to the ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem.
backHtml: coma requires dysfunction of the upper brainstem reticular formation or of both hemispheres.

frontHtml: Identify the neurons most vulnerable to global hypoxic-ischemic injury.
backHtml: after cardiac arrest, hippocampal CA1 neurons, Purkinje cells and deep cortical layers die first.

frontHtml: Recognise bilateral watershed infarction after global hypoperfusion.
backHtml: proximal arm and thigh weakness after profound hypotension means bilateral anterior–middle cerebral watershed infarcts.

frontHtml: Explain the physiological basis of the apnea test: central chemoreceptor sensing of CSF hydrogen ions.
backHtml: the apnea test probes the medullary response to a CO₂-driven fall in CSF pH.

frontHtml: Localise coma with pinpoint pupils and quadriplegia to a pontine hemorrhage.
backHtml: coma with pinpoint pupils and quadriplegia localises to the pons.

frontHtml: Distinguish unresponsive wakefulness from coma, locked-in syndrome, minimally conscious state and brain death.
backHtml: eyes open with sleep–wake cycles but no awareness defines unresponsive wakefulness.

frontHtml: Identify the middle meningeal artery as the source of a temporal epidural hematoma.
backHtml: a biconvex hematoma after temporal bone fracture means epidural bleeding from the middle meningeal artery.

frontHtml: Link chronic subdural hematoma to torn bridging veins in atrophic or anticoagulated older adults.
backHtml: a crescentic collection crossing sutures in an older or anticoagulated patient is a subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins.

frontHtml: Calculate cerebral perfusion pressure from mean arterial pressure and intracranial pressure.
backHtml: CPP equals MAP minus ICP.

frontHtml: Distinguish communicating from obstructive hydrocephalus by which ventricles enlarge.
backHtml: all ventricles enlarged after meningitis means communicating hydrocephalus from scarred arachnoid granulations.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of acetazolamide in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
backHtml: acetazolamide lowers CSF production by inhibiting choroid plexus carbonic anhydrase.

frontHtml: Recognise diffuse axonal injury and its mechanism and histology.
backHtml: deep coma with nearly normal CT after a rotational injury suggests diffuse axonal injury.

frontHtml: Give intravenous thrombolysis to an eligible patient with acute ischemic stroke inside 4.5 hours.
backHtml: a disabling ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, with no hemorrhage and blood pressure below 185/110, gets IV thrombolysis without delay.

frontHtml: Add endovascular thrombectomy for an anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion.
backHtml: large-vessel anterior-circulation occlusion means thrombectomy, even after IV thrombolysis.

frontHtml: Choose a direct oral anticoagulant for secondary prevention after cardioembolic stroke in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
backHtml: stroke with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: a direct oral anticoagulant, started within days.

frontHtml: Use short-term dual antiplatelet therapy after a high-risk TIA without a cardioembolic source.
backHtml: high-risk TIA or minor stroke without a cardiac source: aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 3 weeks, then one antiplatelet drug.

frontHtml: Refer symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis for early carotid endarterectomy.
backHtml: symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70–99% means early endarterectomy, together with best medical therapy.

frontHtml: Reverse warfarin in intracerebral hemorrhage with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K.
backHtml: warfarin-related brain hemorrhage: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K.

frontHtml: Perform lumbar puncture after a normal CT in suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage presenting after 6 hours.
backHtml: thunderclap headache with a normal CT after 6 hours: do a lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: Give oral nimodipine after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia.
backHtml: every patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage gets oral nimodipine for 21 days.

frontHtml: Anticoagulate cerebral venous thrombosis even in the presence of hemorrhagic venous infarction.
backHtml: cerebral venous thrombosis is anticoagulated with heparin even if there is a hemorrhagic venous infarct.

frontHtml: Treat cervical artery dissection with antithrombotic therapy.
backHtml: cervical artery dissection: antithrombotic therapy; stenting only for failure of medical treatment.

frontHtml: Treat hypoglycemic coma immediately with intravenous dextrose.
backHtml: check the fingerstick glucose in every comatose patient and give dextrose for hypoglycemia before anything else.

frontHtml: Recognise the opioid toxidrome and treat with naloxone.
backHtml: coma, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils: ventilate and give naloxone.

frontHtml: Defer and use multimodal assessment for neurological prognosis after cardiac arrest.
backHtml: neurological prognosis after cardiac arrest is multimodal and is not made before about 72 hours.

frontHtml: Correct hypothermia before an evaluation for death by neurologic criteria.
backHtml: correct hypothermia and other confounders before determining death by neurologic criteria.

frontHtml: Interpret a complete brain death evaluation and recognise spinal reflexes as compatible with it.
backHtml: spinal reflexes such as triple flexion are compatible with brain death; they do not mandate an ancillary test.

frontHtml: Recognise locked-in syndrome from a basilar occlusion in a patient labelled unresponsive.
backHtml: always test vertical eye movement and blinking to command before calling a patient unresponsive.

frontHtml: Interpret the cold caloric response in a comatose patient.
backHtml: cold calorics in coma: tonic deviation toward the cold ear means an intact brainstem; no movement means brainstem loss.

frontHtml: Treat an epidural hematoma with mass effect by emergency craniotomy.
backHtml: a symptomatic epidural hematoma with mass effect needs immediate craniotomy.

frontHtml: Drain a symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma with mass effect.
backHtml: a symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma with mass effect is drained, usually through burr holes.

frontHtml: Image the head with CT after minor head trauma in an anticoagulated patient.
backHtml: an anticoagulated patient with a head injury needs a head CT even with a normal examination.

frontHtml: Manage sport-related concussion with removal from play and a graded return.
backHtml: no same-day return to play after a concussion; return is graded and stepwise.

frontHtml: Escalate raised ICP treatment with CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy in traumatic brain injury.
backHtml: first-line treatment of raised ICP after the basics: CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy.

frontHtml: Image with MRI and MR venography before lumbar puncture in suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
backHtml: papilledema needs brain imaging with venography before a lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: Start weight loss and acetazolamide in idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual involvement.
backHtml: idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual change: weight loss plus acetazolamide and visual field monitoring.

frontHtml: Use a high-volume lumbar puncture to select patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus for shunting.
backHtml: suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus: tap test first, then shunt the responders.

frontHtml: Recognise the Cushing reflex and uncal herniation, and treat with osmotherapy and emergency surgery.
backHtml: Cushing reflex with a blown pupil means herniation: osmotherapy and emergency decompression, not antihypertensives.

frontHtml: Diagnose and treat central diabetes insipidus after traumatic brain injury.
backHtml: polyuria with dilute urine and hypernatremia after brain injury is central diabetes insipidus; give desmopressin.

frontHtml: Predict the deficits of a spinal cord hemisection.
backHtml: after a hemisection, weakness and proprioceptive loss are on the side of the lesion and pain loss on the other side.

frontHtml: Identify the functions spared by anterior spinal artery infarction.
backHtml: anterior spinal artery infarction spares the dorsal columns.

frontHtml: Recognise the tract pattern of subacute combined degeneration and its link to nitrous oxide misuse.
backHtml: subacute combined degeneration hits the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves; nitrous oxide can cause it with a normal B 12 level.

frontHtml: Recognise tabes dorsalis as a lesion of the dorsal roots and dorsal columns.
backHtml: tabes dorsalis destroys the dorsal roots and columns: sensory ataxia, areflexia, lightning pains.

frontHtml: Explain the anatomical basis for the level of lumbar puncture.
backHtml: below L2 the subarachnoid space contains roots, not cord.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of bradycardia in autonomic dysreflexia.
backHtml: autonomic dysreflexia pairs reflex hypertension with baroreflex-mediated bradycardia.

frontHtml: Explain why compressive oculomotor palsies affect the pupil.
backHtml: compressive third nerve palsies involve the pupil because the parasympathetic fibres lie on the outside of the nerve.

frontHtml: Identify microvascular ischaemia as the cause of a pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in diabetes.
backHtml: ischaemic third nerve palsy usually spares the pupil.

frontHtml: Identify a trochlear nerve palsy from the pattern of vertical diplopia and head tilt.
backHtml: a fourth nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia on looking down and a head tilt away from the weak eye.

frontHtml: Apply the crossing of the trochlear nerve to localise a nuclear lesion.
backHtml: a trochlear nucleus lesion weakens the opposite superior oblique.

frontHtml: Recognise abducens palsy as a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.
backHtml: abducens palsy can be a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.

frontHtml: Localise a vagus nerve lesion from palatal deviation.
backHtml: the uvula deviates away from the side of a vagus nerve lesion.

frontHtml: Localise a lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion.
backHtml: the tongue deviates toward the side of a hypoglossal lesion; wasting with fasciculations means lower motor neuron.

frontHtml: Relate the anatomy of the cavernous sinus to the order of cranial nerve involvement.
backHtml: the abducens nerve lies free in the cavernous sinus next to the internal carotid artery.

frontHtml: List the cranial nerves that pass through the jugular foramen.
backHtml: the jugular foramen syndrome affects cranial nerves IX, X and XI together.

frontHtml: Predict the deficit from radial nerve injury at the spiral groove.
backHtml: midshaft humerus fracture → radial nerve injury → wrist drop with triceps spared.

frontHtml: Identify anterior interosseous nerve palsy after a supracondylar fracture.
backHtml: anterior interosseous nerve palsy: weak distal flexion of the thumb and index finger, no sensory loss.

frontHtml: Localise an ulnar nerve lesion to Guyon canal from the branches spared.
backHtml: sparing of dorsal hand sensation and long finger flexion localises an ulnar lesion to the wrist.

frontHtml: Predict the deficit after a fibular neck fracture.
backHtml: fibular neck injury → common fibular nerve → foot drop and weak eversion.

frontHtml: Identify femoral neuropathy from an iliopsoas haematoma.
backHtml: an iliopsoas haematoma compresses the femoral nerve: weak quadriceps, lost knee jerk, numb medial leg.

frontHtml: Explain the length-dependent pattern of diabetic polyneuropathy.
backHtml: distal symmetric polyneuropathy starts in the feet because the longest axons fail first.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of carbamazepine in trigeminal neuralgia.
backHtml: carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia by stabilising inactivated sodium channels.

frontHtml: Explain carbamazepine-associated hyponatraemia.
backHtml: carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine cause SIADH-like hyponatraemia; monitor sodium.

frontHtml: Identify the pharmacogenetic test required before carbamazepine.
backHtml: screen for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in at-risk ancestries.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of gabapentinoids in neuropathic pain.
backHtml: gabapentinoids act on the α2δ subunit to reduce excitatory transmitter release.

frontHtml: Localise central post-stroke pain to the sensory thalamus.
backHtml: delayed burning pain in the numb half of the body after a stroke points to the VPL thalamus.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of topical capsaicin.
backHtml: high-dose capsaicin defunctionalises nociceptors through TRPV1 activation.

frontHtml: Distinguish the fibre types carrying first and second pain.
backHtml: first pain travels in A-delta fibres; slow burning pain travels in C fibres.

frontHtml: Distinguish type I from type II complex regional pain syndrome.
backHtml: CRPS type II requires a confirmed nerve injury; type I does not.

frontHtml: Explain how SNRIs relieve neuropathic pain through descending pain modulation.
backHtml: SNRIs and tricyclics relieve neuropathic pain by boosting descending monoaminergic inhibition from the brainstem.

frontHtml: Choose MRI with gadolinium to diagnose a spinal epidural abscess.
backHtml: back pain + fever + neurological deficit → MRI of the whole spine with contrast, then decompression and antibiotics.

frontHtml: Begin immediate glucocorticoids for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression.
backHtml: suspected malignant cord compression with a deficit → dexamethasone now, then emergency MRI and decompression.

frontHtml: Recognise cauda equina syndrome and obtain emergency MRI.
backHtml: saddle anaesthesia plus urinary retention → emergency MRI and decompression.

frontHtml: Manage acute lumbar radiculopathy without red flags conservatively.
backHtml: acute sciatica without red flags: NSAIDs and staying active, no early imaging.

frontHtml: Manage autonomic dysreflexia with positioning and removal of the trigger.
backHtml: autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, loosen clothing, find the trigger (bladder first); drugs only if pressure stays high.

frontHtml: Diagnose central cord syndrome after a hyperextension injury.
backHtml: older adult + hyperextension + hands weaker than legs = central cord syndrome.

frontHtml: Recognise neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.
backHtml: longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis + optic neuritis → test aquaporin-4 IgG.

frontHtml: Confirm degenerative cervical myelopathy with MRI.
backHtml: hand clumsiness + gait imbalance + upper motor neuron signs below the neck → MRI of the cervical spine.

frontHtml: Recognise neurogenic shock after cervical spinal cord injury.
backHtml: hypotension + bradycardia + warm skin after a cervical cord injury = neurogenic shock.

frontHtml: Choose norepinephrine for fluid-refractory neurogenic shock with bradycardia.
backHtml: neurogenic shock not responding to fluids → norepinephrine.

frontHtml: Order emergency vascular imaging for a pupil-involving third nerve palsy.
backHtml: a pupil-involving third nerve palsy needs emergency angiographic imaging.

frontHtml: Diagnose septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
backHtml: bilateral ophthalmoplegia + V1 numbness + fever after a facial infection = cavernous sinus thrombosis.

frontHtml: Distinguish monocular from binocular diplopia and choose the right next step.
backHtml: monocular diplopia is an eye problem; binocular diplopia is a nerve, muscle or junction problem.

frontHtml: Investigate a new abducens palsy with papilledema in a child with brain MRI.
backHtml: a new abducens palsy with papilledema and ataxia in a child → MRI for a posterior fossa mass.

frontHtml: Investigate unexplained recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with CT of the neck and chest.
backHtml: unexplained left vocal fold paralysis → CT of the neck and chest along the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

frontHtml: Recognise spinal accessory nerve injury after posterior triangle surgery.
backHtml: posterior triangle surgery + weak shrug and shoulder droop = spinal accessory nerve injury.

frontHtml: Identify hypoglossal nerve injury after carotid endarterectomy.
backHtml: after carotid surgery, tongue deviation toward the operated side means hypoglossal nerve injury.

frontHtml: Give glucocorticoids first in pituitary apoplexy with cranial neuropathy and hypotension.
backHtml: pituitary apoplexy with hypotension → IV hydrocortisone first, then MRI and neurosurgery.

frontHtml: Manage mild carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy with night splinting.
backHtml: mild carpal tunnel syndrome, especially in pregnancy: night splints first.

frontHtml: Refer carpal tunnel syndrome with axonal loss for surgical release.
backHtml: carpal tunnel syndrome with thenar wasting or severe conduction findings → surgical release.

frontHtml: Recognise polyarteritis nodosa as a cause of mononeuritis multiplex.
backHtml: mononeuritis multiplex + hepatitis B + hypertension + ANCA-negative = polyarteritis nodosa.

frontHtml: Apply the timing of diabetic neuropathy screening.
backHtml: screen for diabetic neuropathy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and every year after.

frontHtml: Distinguish common fibular neuropathy from L5 radiculopathy.
backHtml: foot drop with normal inversion and hip abduction = common fibular neuropathy, not L5.

frontHtml: Manage meralgia paresthetica conservatively.
backHtml: meralgia paresthetica: remove the compression and reassure.

frontHtml: Choose conservative management for mild ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
backHtml: mild ulnar neuropathy at the elbow → avoid pressure and flexion, night splint.

frontHtml: Choose the highest-yield tests for distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
backHtml: first-line tests in distal symmetric polyneuropathy: glucose tolerance, B 12 and immunofixation.

frontHtml: Treat classic trigeminal neuralgia with carbamazepine.
backHtml: carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

frontHtml: Recognise red flags for secondary trigeminal neuralgia and obtain MRI.
backHtml: young age, sensory loss or bilateral pain in trigeminal neuralgia → MRI for MS or a structural cause.

frontHtml: Choose microvascular decompression for refractory trigeminal neuralgia.
backHtml: drug-refractory trigeminal neuralgia with neurovascular compression in a fit patient → microvascular decompression.

frontHtml: Choose topical lidocaine for postherpetic neuralgia in a frail older adult.
backHtml: localised postherpetic neuralgia in an older adult → topical lidocaine.

frontHtml: Recommend the recombinant zoster vaccine for adults aged 50 and older.
backHtml: adults ≥50: recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses.

frontHtml: Begin graded rehabilitation for complex regional pain syndrome.
backHtml: CRPS: early graded rehabilitation is the cornerstone of treatment.

frontHtml: Choose duloxetine for painful diabetic neuropathy with comorbid depression.
backHtml: painful diabetic neuropathy + depression → duloxetine.

frontHtml: Choose a neuropathic pain drug according to comorbidities in an older adult.
backHtml: in older adults with urinary retention or conduction disease, prefer a gabapentinoid (or SNRI) over a tricyclic.

frontHtml: Identify neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau as the intracellular lesion of Alzheimer disease.
backHtml: Alzheimer disease has two lesions: extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau tangles.

frontHtml: Relate APP gene dosage on chromosome 21 to early Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.
backHtml: Three copies of APP (chromosome 21) explain early Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.

frontHtml: Explain bradycardia and syncope caused by cholinesterase inhibitors used in dementia.
backHtml: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia and syncope through increased vagal tone.

frontHtml: Identify the NMDA receptor as the target of memantine.
backHtml: Memantine is an open-channel NMDA receptor blocker used in moderate to severe Alzheimer disease.

frontHtml: Recognise behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia and its imaging pattern.
backHtml: Personality change before memory loss points to frontotemporal dementia and frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

frontHtml: Link the clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies to cortical alpha-synuclein inclusions.
backHtml: Fluctuations, visual hallucinations and dream enactment point to Lewy body dementia; avoid typical antipsychotics.

frontHtml: Localise Korsakoff amnesia to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.
backHtml: Korsakoff syndrome is amnesia with confabulation from thiamine-related damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.

frontHtml: Localise amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to upper and lower motor neurons.
backHtml: ALS combines upper and lower motor neuron signs with spared sensation, eye movements and sphincters.

frontHtml: State the mechanism of riluzole in ALS.
backHtml: Riluzole limits glutamate excitotoxicity and modestly prolongs survival in ALS.

frontHtml: Explain how nusinersen increases SMN protein in spinal muscular atrophy.
backHtml: Nusinersen and risdiplam correct SMN2 splicing; onasemnogene replaces SMN1.

frontHtml: Explain the reading-frame rule that separates Becker from Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
backHtml: In-frame dystrophin deletions give Becker; frameshift deletions give Duchenne.

frontHtml: Identify the repeat expansion that causes myotonic dystrophy type 1.
backHtml: Myotonia plus cataracts, ptosis and heart block means myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DMPK CTG repeat); congenital cases come from affected mothers.

frontHtml: Explain molecular mimicry as the mechanism of Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter infection.
backHtml: Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter is molecular mimicry against nerve gangliosides.

frontHtml: State the mechanism and purpose of carbidopa in levodopa therapy.
backHtml: Carbidopa blocks peripheral decarboxylation of levodopa and does not enter the brain.

frontHtml: Identify alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies as the pathological hallmark of Parkinson disease.
backHtml: Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease are alpha-synuclein inclusions in nigral neurons.

frontHtml: Recognise impulse control disorders as an adverse effect of dopamine agonists.
backHtml: Dopamine agonists can cause compulsive gambling and shopping; screen for it.

frontHtml: Explain paternal anticipation in Huntington disease.
backHtml: Huntington anticipation comes from CAG expansion in the male germline.

frontHtml: Identify the ATP7B defect in Wilson disease presenting with neurological features.
backHtml: Wilson disease is loss of hepatocyte ATP7B: low ceruloplasmin, copper in liver, brain and cornea.

frontHtml: Identify VMAT2 inhibition as the mechanism of tetrabenazine and its key adverse effect.
backHtml: VMAT2 inhibitors treat Huntington chorea; watch for depression and suicidality.

frontHtml: Name the thiamine-dependent enzyme used to assess thiamine deficiency.
backHtml: Erythrocyte transketolase activity is a functional test of thiamine status.

frontHtml: Distinguish Tay-Sachs disease from Niemann-Pick disease by the presence of organomegaly.
backHtml: Cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly means Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A).

frontHtml: Identify very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
backHtml: Adrenal insufficiency plus white matter disease in a boy means X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and VLCFA build-up.

frontHtml: Interpret methylmalonic acid and homocysteine in cobalamin deficiency myelopathy.
backHtml: Functional B12 deficiency raises both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; folate deficiency raises only homocysteine.

frontHtml: Describe the pathology and timing of osmotic demyelination syndrome.
backHtml: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast destroys pontine myelin days later.

frontHtml: Explain how lactulose lowers ammonia absorption in hepatic encephalopathy.
backHtml: Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia as ammonium.

frontHtml: Explain astrocyte swelling in hepatic encephalopathy.
backHtml: In hepatic encephalopathy, astrocytes swell from glutamine made while detoxifying ammonia.

frontHtml: Recognise MELAS and its muscle biopsy hallmark.
backHtml: Ragged red fibres on muscle biopsy suggest a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy such as MELAS.

frontHtml: Order the standard laboratory evaluation for reversible causes of cognitive decline.
backHtml: Check B12 and TSH (and image the brain) before specialised biomarkers.

frontHtml: Use the lumbar tap test to evaluate suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus.
backHtml: Suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus: do a large-volume tap test to select patients for a shunt.

frontHtml: Choose a cholinesterase inhibitor for hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies.
backHtml: Treat hallucinations in Lewy body dementia with a cholinesterase inhibitor first; avoid typical antipsychotics.

frontHtml: Identify baseline MRI as required safety screening before anti-amyloid antibody therapy.
backHtml: Anti-amyloid antibodies require a baseline MRI and MRI monitoring for ARIA.

frontHtml: Manage behavioural symptoms of dementia by treating triggers and using non-drug measures first.
backHtml: Agitation in dementia: search for triggers such as pain or constipation and use non-drug measures first.

frontHtml: Distinguish depression with cognitive symptoms from dementia and choose first-line treatment.
backHtml: Depression in older adults can mimic dementia; treat with an SSRI and reassess cognition.

frontHtml: Recognise transient global amnesia and distinguish it from TIA and seizure.
backHtml: Hours of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning and a normal exam: transient global amnesia.

frontHtml: Recognise impending neuromuscular respiratory failure in myasthenic crisis and secure the airway.
backHtml: Intubate a myasthenic or Guillain-Barré patient when FVC falls below about 20 mL/kg, NIF weakens past −30, or secretions pool.

frontHtml: Order chest imaging for thymoma after diagnosing myasthenia gravis.
backHtml: Every new diagnosis of myasthenia gravis needs chest imaging for thymoma.

frontHtml: Identify antibiotics that can worsen myasthenia gravis.
backHtml: Avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and macrolides in myasthenia gravis when an alternative exists.

frontHtml: Choose lumbar puncture to support a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
backHtml: Suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome: do a lumbar puncture looking for albuminocytologic dissociation.

frontHtml: Select immunotherapy for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
backHtml: Treat Guillain-Barré syndrome with IVIG or plasma exchange, not steroids.

frontHtml: Decide on elective intubation in Guillain-Barré syndrome using FVC and NIF.
backHtml: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, intubate on falling FVC and NIF, not on desaturation.

frontHtml: Manage suspected infant botulism.
backHtml: Treat suspected infant botulism with human botulism immune globulin; avoid aminoglycosides.

frontHtml: Start noninvasive ventilation for respiratory insufficiency in ALS.
backHtml: Start noninvasive ventilation in ALS when FVC falls below about 50% or orthopnea appears.

frontHtml: Choose genetic testing to confirm Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
backHtml: Confirm suspected Duchenne muscular dystrophy with dystrophin gene testing, not biopsy.

frontHtml: Search for small cell lung cancer in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
backHtml: Lambert-Eaton syndrome in a smoker: search for small cell lung cancer.

frontHtml: Select initial therapy for Parkinson disease in an older adult.
backHtml: Carbidopa-levodopa is first choice for Parkinson disease that impairs function, especially in older adults.

frontHtml: Manage drug-induced psychosis in Parkinson disease.
backHtml: Parkinson disease psychosis: stop anticholinergics first; keep levodopa; avoid typical antipsychotics.

frontHtml: Treat end-of-dose wearing off in Parkinson disease.
backHtml: Wearing off: shorten the dosing interval or add a COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor or dopamine agonist.

frontHtml: Treat essential tremor in a patient with a contraindication to propranolol.
backHtml: Essential tremor: propranolol or primidone; choose primidone in asthma.

frontHtml: Select treatment for tardive dyskinesia.
backHtml: Treat tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor; anticholinergics make it worse.

frontHtml: Treat an acute dystonic reaction to an antipsychotic.
backHtml: Acute dystonia after an antipsychotic: give IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine.

frontHtml: Choose first-line treatment for Tourette syndrome.
backHtml: Behavioural therapy is first-line for tics that cause distress in Tourette syndrome.

frontHtml: Arrange appropriate counseling before predictive testing for Huntington disease.
backHtml: Predictive Huntington testing in adults requires pre-test genetic counseling.

frontHtml: Distinguish progressive supranuclear palsy from Parkinson disease.
backHtml: Early falls plus impaired downgaze and a poor levodopa response suggests progressive supranuclear palsy.

frontHtml: Treat severe symptomatic hyponatremia with hypertonic saline.
backHtml: Seizures from hyponatremia: give 3% saline boluses for a quick 4–6 mEq/L rise, then cap the daily rise.

frontHtml: Manage overcorrection of chronic hyponatremia to prevent osmotic demyelination.
backHtml: If sodium overshoots in a high-risk patient, re-lower it with dextrose water and desmopressin.

frontHtml: Begin treatment of hepatic encephalopathy and identify its precipitant.
backHtml: Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose plus a search for the trigger (infection, bleeding, drugs, dehydration).

frontHtml: Prevent recurrent hepatic encephalopathy with rifaximin.
backHtml: Recurrent hepatic encephalopathy on lactulose: add rifaximin.

frontHtml: Treat B12-deficiency myelopathy after bariatric surgery.
backHtml: B12 deficiency with neurological signs: give intramuscular cobalamin promptly, even if the hemoglobin is normal.

frontHtml: Recognise copper deficiency myelopathy from zinc excess.
backHtml: A B12-like myeloneuropathy with normal B12 and cytopenias: check copper (zinc excess, bariatric surgery).

frontHtml: Plan surveillance for asymptomatic X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
backHtml: Asymptomatic X-ALD: monitor adrenals and brain MRI so transplant can be offered at the first MRI change.

frontHtml: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy safely in a hypoglycemic patient.
backHtml: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine before or with glucose, without waiting for tests.

frontHtml: Identify uremic encephalopathy as an indication for urgent dialysis.
backHtml: Uremic encephalopathy or pericarditis is an indication for urgent dialysis.

frontHtml: Relate the thalamic T-type calcium current to absence seizures and to the mechanism of ethosuximide.
backHtml: absence seizures (3-per-second spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation) respond to ethosuximide, a thalamic T-type calcium channel blocker.

frontHtml: Identify the EEG pattern of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
backHtml: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy pairs morning myoclonus with generalized polyspike-and-wave on EEG.

frontHtml: Identify the receptor target of lasmiditan and why it is safe in vascular disease.
backHtml: lasmiditan (5-HT 1F ) and the gepants (CGRP receptor antagonists) are acute options when triptans are contraindicated by vascular disease.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of migraine aura.
backHtml: a gradually spreading visual aura with positive then negative symptoms is migraine aura from cortical spreading depolarization.

frontHtml: Match levetiracetam to its mechanism and characteristic adverse effect.
backHtml: levetiracetam = SV2A binding, renal clearance, few interactions, mood and behaviour side effects.

frontHtml: Distinguish benzodiazepine and barbiturate actions on the GABA A receptor.
backHtml: benzodiazepines increase opening frequency; barbiturates increase opening duration.

frontHtml: Trace the parasympathetic pathway that causes tearing in cluster headache.
backHtml: the autonomic signs of cluster headache are a trigeminal-parasympathetic reflex through the facial nerve and the pterygopalatine ganglion.

frontHtml: Distinguish receptor-targeting from ligand-targeting CGRP monoclonal antibodies.
backHtml: erenumab blocks the CGRP receptor; the other CGRP antibodies bind the peptide.

frontHtml: Recognize the pathology of mesial temporal sclerosis.
backHtml: drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy is most often due to hippocampal sclerosis (CA1 neuron loss and gliosis).

frontHtml: Give a benzodiazepine first in status epilepticus, choosing the route by IV access.
backHtml: status epilepticus is treated first with a benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam if there is no IV access.

frontHtml: Choose an IV second-line drug when status epilepticus continues after benzodiazepines.
backHtml: benzodiazepine-resistant status epilepticus needs IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.

frontHtml: Recognize when to evaluate for nonconvulsive status epilepticus after convulsions stop.
backHtml: if consciousness does not return after convulsive status, get an EEG to look for nonconvulsive status.

frontHtml: Choose the standard evaluation of a first unprovoked seizure.
backHtml: unprovoked first seizure: labs, then brain MRI and EEG.

frontHtml: Manage antiseizure therapy in a woman planning pregnancy.
backHtml: avoid valproate in anyone who could become pregnant; switch before conception.

frontHtml: Select contraception for a woman with migraine with aura.
backHtml: migraine with aura is a contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception.

frontHtml: Treat an acute cluster headache attack.
backHtml: acute cluster headache: high-flow oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan; prevention with verapamil.

frontHtml: Diagnose and manage medication-overuse headache.
backHtml: near-daily headache with frequent analgesic use is medication-overuse headache: withdraw and start prevention.

frontHtml: Manage a simple febrile seizure without unnecessary investigation.
backHtml: simple febrile seizure in a well, vaccinated child: reassurance and education, no routine tests.

frontHtml: Choose video-EEG to diagnose psychogenic nonepileptic seizures.
backHtml: suspected functional seizures are confirmed by capturing a typical event on video-EEG.

frontHtml: Identify orexin neuron loss as the cause of narcolepsy with cataplexy.
backHtml: narcolepsy type 1 = loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons, low CSF orexin, cataplexy.

frontHtml: Link REM sleep behavior disorder to α-synuclein neurodegeneration.
backHtml: REM sleep behavior disorder is a prodrome of α-synucleinopathies.

frontHtml: Describe the neural pathway controlling melatonin secretion and the action of ramelteon.
backHtml: melatonin release is set by retina → SCN → sympathetic chain (superior cervical ganglion) → pineal.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of orexin receptor antagonists.
backHtml: orexin antagonists (-orexants) treat insomnia; they are contraindicated in narcolepsy.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes respiration in heart failure.
backHtml: Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure comes from delayed, overly sensitive ventilatory control (high loop gain).

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of sodium oxybate in narcolepsy.
backHtml: sodium oxybate (GHB) is a GABA B agonist that treats cataplexy.

frontHtml: Choose cognitive behavioural therapy as first-line treatment of chronic insomnia.
backHtml: CBT-I is first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.

frontHtml: Order the correct test sequence for suspected narcolepsy.
backHtml: narcolepsy is confirmed by polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test.

frontHtml: Treat iron deficiency first in restless legs syndrome.
backHtml: check iron in restless legs syndrome and replace it when ferritin is 75 ng/mL or less.

frontHtml: Recognize and manage augmentation in restless legs syndrome.
backHtml: augmentation on a dopamine agonist: taper it and switch to an α2δ ligand.

frontHtml: Confirm suspected REM sleep behavior disorder with polysomnography.
backHtml: REM sleep behavior disorder is confirmed by polysomnography showing REM sleep without atonia.

frontHtml: Manage delayed sleep-wake phase disorder in an adolescent.
backHtml: delayed sleep phase: morning light and early-evening melatonin; advanced phase: evening light.

frontHtml: Choose CPAP as first-line treatment for symptomatic severe obstructive sleep apnea.
backHtml: symptomatic moderate-severe OSA is treated with CPAP plus weight loss.

frontHtml: Select a treatment for cataplexy in narcolepsy.
backHtml: for cataplexy, use sodium oxybate (or a REM-suppressing antidepressant); modafinil treats sleepiness only.

frontHtml: Explain the disproportionate rise in phenytoin levels with dose increases.
backHtml: phenytoin has saturable (zero-order) kinetics: small dose changes can cause large level changes.

frontHtml: Identify the pharmacogenetic marker for carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN.
backHtml: screen for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in patients of Asian ancestry.

frontHtml: Relate vincristine's mechanism to its neurotoxicity.
backHtml: vincristine blocks microtubule assembly: neuropathy and constipation, little marrow suppression.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of isoniazid-induced seizures and their treatment.
backHtml: isoniazid seizures resist benzodiazepines because GABA synthesis falls; give IV pyridoxine.

frontHtml: Explain the valproate-lamotrigine interaction and its link to rash.
backHtml: valproate raises lamotrigine levels; start lamotrigine low and slow to avoid serious rash.

frontHtml: Link topiramate's carbonic anhydrase inhibition to its adverse effects.
backHtml: topiramate: carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes acidosis and calcium phosphate stones; also weight loss and word-finding difficulty.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of VMAT2 inhibitors in tardive dyskinesia.
backHtml: VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia by depleting presynaptic dopamine.

frontHtml: Explain why antimuscarinic drugs relieve drug-induced acute dystonia.
backHtml: acute dystonia from D 2 blockers responds to antimuscarinic drugs (benztropine or diphenhydramine).

frontHtml: Explain linezolid-associated serotonin syndrome.
backHtml: linezolid is an MAO inhibitor; with SSRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome.

frontHtml: Manage neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
backHtml: neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate; dantrolene or bromocriptine if severe.

frontHtml: Manage serotonin syndrome caused by an SSRI-tramadol interaction.
backHtml: serotonin syndrome: stop serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if not settling.

frontHtml: Treat drug-induced acute dystonia.
backHtml: acute dystonia after a dopamine antagonist: IV diphenhydramine or benztropine.

frontHtml: Manage tardive dyskinesia in a patient who must remain on an antipsychotic.
backHtml: tardive dyskinesia on a needed antipsychotic: add a VMAT2 inhibitor; avoid anticholinergics.

frontHtml: Recognize phenytoin toxicity hidden by hypoalbuminemia.
backHtml: in hypoalbuminemia, phenytoin toxicity can occur with a normal total level: check the free level.

frontHtml: Avoid flumazenil and manage mixed benzodiazepine-tricyclic overdose safely.
backHtml: avoid flumazenil in benzodiazepine dependence or tricyclic co-ingestion; support the airway and treat the tricyclic.

frontHtml: Recognize and manage tacrolimus-associated PRES.
backHtml: PRES (calcineurin inhibitor, hypertension, posterior edema): lower BP and stop or change the drug.

frontHtml: Manage anticholinergic delirium in an older adult by deprescribing.
backHtml: in older adults, new confusion with anticholinergic signs calls for deprescribing the culprits.

frontHtml: Choose duloxetine for painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.
backHtml: duloxetine is the drug of choice for painful chemotherapy-induced neuropathy.

frontHtml: Prevent isoniazid neuropathy with pyridoxine in high-risk patients.
backHtml: give pyridoxine with isoniazid when there are risk factors for neuropathy.

frontHtml: Recognize and manage valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy.
backHtml: valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy with normal liver tests: stop it and give levocarnitine.

frontHtml: Identify drugs that exacerbate myasthenia gravis.
backHtml: fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides can trigger myasthenic crises.

frontHtml: Identify Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the cause of hyperacute neonatal conjunctivitis from its timing and Gram stain.
backHtml: neonatal conjunctivitis in days 2–5 with gram-negative diplococci is gonococcal.

frontHtml: Recognise neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis and its association with later afebrile pneumonia.
backHtml: neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis needs systemic treatment because it can be followed by afebrile pneumonia.

frontHtml: Identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the classic cause of contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis.
backHtml: contact lens wearer plus rapidly progressive corneal ulcer equals Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Associate acute anterior uveitis with HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis.
backHtml: anterior uveitis plus inflammatory back pain points to HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis.

frontHtml: Explain the usual route of spread of sinus infection into the orbit.
backHtml: orbital cellulitis in a child usually comes from the ethmoid sinus through the medial orbital wall.

frontHtml: Describe the venous route by which orbital infection causes cavernous sinus thrombosis.
backHtml: orbital or mid-face infection reaches the cavernous sinus through valveless ophthalmic veins.

frontHtml: State the site of latency of herpes simplex virus that causes recurrent keratitis.
backHtml: HSV keratitis recurs from latency in the trigeminal ganglion.

frontHtml: Describe the normal function of the RB protein in cell cycle control.
backHtml: RB holds E2F in check at the G1–S checkpoint until it is phosphorylated.

frontHtml: Recognise osteosarcoma as the characteristic second cancer after heritable retinoblastoma.
backHtml: survivors of heritable retinoblastoma are at risk of osteosarcoma.

frontHtml: Apply the two-hit model to distinguish heritable from nonheritable retinoblastoma.
backHtml: bilateral or multifocal retinoblastoma implies a germline RB1 mutation.

frontHtml: State the characteristic metastatic site of uveal melanoma and the reason it spreads through blood.
backHtml: uveal melanoma metastasises to the liver.

frontHtml: Recognise eyelid basal cell carcinoma and its histological features.
backHtml: the most common eyelid cancer is basal cell carcinoma, with palisading basaloid nests.

frontHtml: Recognise sebaceous gland carcinoma as a mimic of recurrent chalazion.
backHtml: a chalazion that keeps recurring in an older adult is sebaceous carcinoma until a biopsy says otherwise.

frontHtml: Recognise choroidal metastasis as the most common intraocular malignancy in adults.
backHtml: multiple creamy choroidal lesions in a patient with cancer are metastases.

frontHtml: Explain the optics of myopia and its correction.
backHtml: myopia focuses in front of the retina and is corrected with a minus lens.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of presbyopia.
backHtml: presbyopia is age-related loss of lens elasticity, which limits accommodation.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism and adverse effects of prostaglandin analogue eye drops.
backHtml: prostaglandin analogues raise uveoscleral outflow and can darken the iris and lengthen lashes.

frontHtml: Explain how anticholinergic drugs precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma.
backHtml: anticholinergic mydriasis can precipitate angle closure in a narrow-angled eye.

frontHtml: Distinguish cystathionine β-synthase deficiency from other causes of lens disease and hyperhomocysteinaemia.
backHtml: lens dislocation with thrombosis and high methionine points to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the biochemical basis of cataracts in disorders of galactose metabolism.
backHtml: galactitol formed by aldose reductase causes the cataracts of galactose disorders.

frontHtml: Associate long-term corticosteroid use with posterior subcapsular cataract.
backHtml: chronic glucocorticoids cause posterior subcapsular cataract.

frontHtml: Interpret the swinging-flashlight test to localise an afferent pupillary defect.
backHtml: both pupils dilating when light swings to one eye means an afferent lesion of that eye's optic nerve.

frontHtml: Localise Horner syndrome from a Pancoast tumour to the second-order sympathetic neuron.
backHtml: Horner syndrome with an apical lung mass is a second-order (preganglionic) lesion.

frontHtml: Explain why compressive oculomotor palsies involve the pupil.
backHtml: a “blown” pupil with an oculomotor palsy means compression until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Localise internuclear ophthalmoplegia to the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
backHtml: an INO is named by the eye that fails to adduct; the lesion is in that side's MLF.

frontHtml: Recognise a tonic pupil and localise it to the ciliary ganglion.
backHtml: a large pupil that constricts to dilute pilocarpine is a tonic pupil from ciliary ganglion damage.

frontHtml: Manage suspected contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis.
backHtml: contact lens ulcer: no patch, no steroid, antipseudomonal drops and same-day ophthalmology.

frontHtml: Treat neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis with systemic ceftriaxone.
backHtml: neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis needs systemic ceftriaxone, not drops alone.

frontHtml: Distinguish scleritis from episcleritis and arrange urgent systemic treatment.
backHtml: scleritis needs urgent ophthalmology and systemic anti-inflammatory therapy.

frontHtml: Distinguish orbital from preseptal cellulitis and manage orbital cellulitis.
backHtml: orbital signs mean IV antibiotics and contrast CT, not oral treatment.

frontHtml: Diagnose anterior uveitis and recognise its association with inflammatory bowel disease.
backHtml: ciliary flush plus photophobia plus a small pupil is anterior uveitis.

frontHtml: Manage acute postoperative endophthalmitis with intravitreal antibiotics.
backHtml: postoperative endophthalmitis needs intravitreal antibiotics immediately.

frontHtml: Manage herpes zoster ophthalmicus with oral antiviral therapy and ophthalmology review.
backHtml: zoster in V1, especially on the nose, needs an oral antiviral and an eye examination.

frontHtml: Refer urgently a child with leukocoria.
backHtml: an absent or white red reflex means urgent ophthalmology referral.

frontHtml: Arrange germline testing and sibling screening after a diagnosis of bilateral retinoblastoma.
backHtml: bilateral retinoblastoma calls for germline testing and screening of siblings.

frontHtml: Choose MRI rather than CT to stage retinoblastoma.
backHtml: stage retinoblastoma with MRI, not CT.

frontHtml: Stage uveal melanoma with liver imaging.
backHtml: uveal melanoma staging and follow-up focus on the liver.

frontHtml: Biopsy an eyelid lesion with features of basal cell carcinoma.
backHtml: an eyelid lesion with lash loss, ulceration or pearly edges needs a biopsy.

frontHtml: Biopsy a recurrent chalazion in an older adult to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.
backHtml: biopsy a recurrent chalazion in an older adult.

frontHtml: Recognise ocular adnexal marginal zone lymphoma.
backHtml: a salmon-patch orbital or conjunctival mass in an older adult is lymphoma until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Start immediate pressure-lowering treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma.
backHtml: angle closure: drops plus acetazolamide immediately, then laser iridotomy.

frontHtml: Recommend prophylactic laser iridotomy of the fellow eye after acute angle closure.
backHtml: after angle closure, treat the other eye with a prophylactic iridotomy.

frontHtml: Choose first-line treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and recognise β-blocker contraindications.
backHtml: open-angle glaucoma: prostaglandin analogue first; avoid topical β-blockers in asthma.

frontHtml: Refer for cataract surgery when cataract impairs function.
backHtml: cataract that limits daily activities is treated surgically.

frontHtml: Manage a typical chalazion conservatively.
backHtml: treat a typical chalazion with warm compresses first.

frontHtml: Recognise topiramate-induced bilateral angle closure.
backHtml: new bilateral angle closure with myopia in the first weeks of topiramate is a drug reaction.

frontHtml: Evaluate dry eye with dry mouth for Sjögren syndrome.
backHtml: dry eyes plus dry mouth: check anti-Ro and anti-La.

frontHtml: Order emergency vascular imaging for a pupil-involving oculomotor palsy.
backHtml: painful oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil: emergency vascular imaging.

frontHtml: Investigate acute painful Horner syndrome for carotid artery dissection.
backHtml: painful Horner syndrome is carotid dissection until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Treat active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease.
backHtml: active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease is treated with IV glucocorticoid pulses.

frontHtml: Treat anisometropic amblyopia by occluding the stronger eye.
backHtml: treat amblyopia by correcting the refraction and then patching or blurring the good eye.

frontHtml: Distinguish pseudostrabismus from true strabismus in an infant.
backHtml: symmetric light reflexes and a normal cover test mean pseudostrabismus.

frontHtml: Investigate internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult with MRI.
backHtml: an INO in a young adult calls for MRI looking for demyelination.

frontHtml: Use pharmacological testing to localise Horner syndrome.
backHtml: a Horner pupil that will not dilate with hydroxyamphetamine has a postganglionic lesion.

frontHtml: Explain the cherry-red spot of central retinal artery occlusion from the dual blood supply of the retina.
backHtml: the cherry-red spot is normal choroid seen through the thin fovea, surrounded by whitened inner retina.

frontHtml: Identify pericyte loss as the earliest microvascular lesion of diabetic retinopathy.
backHtml: pericyte loss is the earliest histological change in diabetic retinopathy, and microaneurysms are the earliest clinical sign.

frontHtml: Relate retinal neovascularization to VEGF and identify the target of intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs.
backHtml: intravitreal anti-VEGF agents treat proliferative diabetic retinopathy and macular oedema by blocking the hypoxia-driven growth signal.

frontHtml: Identify rod photoreceptors as the primary target in retinitis pigmentosa from its presentation.
backHtml: retinitis pigmentosa starts in the rods, so night blindness and peripheral field loss come before central loss.

frontHtml: Describe the two-phase pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity.
backHtml: retinopathy of prematurity is a two-phase disease: oxygen-induced arrest of vessel growth, then hypoxia-driven VEGF-mediated proliferation.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of visual distortion in neovascular age-related macular degeneration.
backHtml: sudden metamorphopsia in an older patient with drusen means choroidal neovascularization until proved otherwise.

frontHtml: Identify the vascular basis of arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
backHtml: in giant cell arteritis, blindness usually results from occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve head.

frontHtml: Recognize CMV retinitis and explain ganciclovir activation and resistance.
backHtml: ganciclovir needs the CMV UL97 kinase for activation, so UL97 mutations cause resistance.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of papilloedema.
backHtml: papilloedema is axonal swelling from stasis of axoplasmic flow caused by raised intracranial pressure, usually bilateral with preserved acuity.

frontHtml: Contrast the tissue injury mechanisms of alkali and acid burns of the eye.
backHtml: alkali burns of the eye are usually worse than acid burns because liquefactive necrosis lets the chemical keep penetrating.

frontHtml: Identify the muscle and nerve involved in an orbital floor fracture.
backHtml: limited upgaze plus cheek numbness after blunt orbital trauma means an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment.

frontHtml: Describe the afferent and efferent limbs of the oculocardiac reflex.
backHtml: the oculocardiac reflex is trigeminal in and vagal out.

frontHtml: Identify the sensory innervation of the cornea.
backHtml: corneal pain and the afferent limb of the corneal reflex travel in V1.

frontHtml: Explain why hyphema is more dangerous in sickle cell disease or trait.
backHtml: in sickle cell disease or trait, rigid sickled red cells block aqueous outflow and make a hyphema more dangerous.

frontHtml: Identify the structure released in lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
backHtml: orbital compartment syndrome is relieved by releasing the lateral canthal tendon.

frontHtml: Identify the usual sites of globe rupture after blunt trauma.
backHtml: blunt globe rupture occurs at the thinnest sclera, behind the rectus insertions or at the limbus.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of topiramate-induced angle closure.
backHtml: topiramate causes bilateral angle closure through ciliochoroidal effusion, not pupillary block.

frontHtml: Relate tamsulosin's receptor selectivity to intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.
backHtml: alpha-1A blockade by tamsulosin weakens the iris dilator and causes floppy iris during cataract surgery.

frontHtml: Explain the visual side effect of PDE5 inhibitors.
backHtml: PDE5 inhibitors cross-inhibit retinal PDE6 and tint vision blue.

frontHtml: Identify the main risk factors for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy.
backHtml: keep hydroxychloroquine at 5 mg/kg/day of actual body weight or less to limit retinal toxicity.

frontHtml: Recognize systemic adverse effects of topical timolol.
backHtml: topical timolol can cause systemic beta-blockade, so avoid it in asthma and bradycardia.

frontHtml: Recognize ethambutol optic neuropathy.
backHtml: new red-green colour loss in a patient on tuberculosis treatment means ethambutol optic neuropathy.

frontHtml: Recognize the visual field toxicity of vigabatrin.
backHtml: vigabatrin can cause permanent peripheral field loss; monitor visual fields.

frontHtml: Identify the cataract type caused by glucocorticoids.
backHtml: glucocorticoids cause posterior subcapsular cataract and can raise eye pressure.

frontHtml: Manage acute central retinal artery occlusion as a stroke equivalent.
backHtml: treat central retinal artery occlusion as a stroke: immediate referral to a stroke centre.

frontHtml: Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately for giant cell arteritis with visual loss.
backHtml: in giant cell arteritis with visual loss, give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and confirm the diagnosis afterward.

frontHtml: Apply retinopathy screening timing in type 2 diabetes.
backHtml: screen for retinopathy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and within 5 years of type 1.

frontHtml: Choose anti-VEGF therapy for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision.
backHtml: centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with visual loss: intravitreal anti-VEGF first.

frontHtml: Treat neovascular age-related macular degeneration with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy.
backHtml: wet AMD is treated urgently with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

frontHtml: Recommend the AREDS2-type supplement for intermediate age-related macular degeneration in a smoker.
backHtml: intermediate AMD: stop smoking and take an AREDS2-type supplement without beta-carotene.

frontHtml: Recognize retinal detachment and arrange same-day ophthalmology.
backHtml: flashes, floaters and a curtain mean retinal detachment and same-day ophthalmology.

frontHtml: Treat CMV retinitis in advanced HIV.
backHtml: CMV retinitis is treated with valganciclovir (plus intravitreal therapy if sight-threatening) and prompt antiretroviral therapy.

frontHtml: Apply screening criteria for retinopathy of prematurity.
backHtml: screen for retinopathy of prematurity at 30 weeks or less or 1,500 g or less.

frontHtml: Evaluate optic neuritis with MRI of the brain and orbits.
backHtml: optic neuritis needs gadolinium MRI of the brain and orbits to assess for multiple sclerosis.

frontHtml: Irrigate immediately as the first step in chemical eye injury.
backHtml: in a chemical eye injury, irrigate first and examine later.

frontHtml: Use tear-film pH to guide the endpoint of irrigation after a chemical injury.
backHtml: irrigate a chemical injury until the tear pH is neutral, and remove retained particles.

frontHtml: Identify limbal ischaemia as the main prognostic sign in chemical eye injury.
backHtml: the extent of limbal whitening is the key prognostic sign after a chemical burn.

frontHtml: Treat a contact lens-related corneal abrasion with anti-pseudomonal cover and no patching.
backHtml: a lens-related corneal abrasion needs anti-pseudomonal drops and no patch.

frontHtml: Manage a suspected open globe injury.
backHtml: open globe: shield, antiemetic, antibiotics, CT, and nothing that touches or presses the eye.

frontHtml: Avoid acetazolamide in hyphema with sickle cell disease or trait.
backHtml: avoid systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors in hyphema with sickle cell disease or trait.

frontHtml: Recognize the trapdoor orbital floor fracture with oculocardiac reflex as a surgical emergency.
backHtml: a child with an orbital floor fracture, entrapment and oculocardiac reflex needs urgent surgery.

frontHtml: Perform emergency lateral canthotomy for orbital compartment syndrome.
backHtml: orbital compartment syndrome needs bedside canthotomy and cantholysis before imaging.

frontHtml: Choose CT to look for a metallic intraocular foreign body.
backHtml: suspected metallic intraocular foreign body: CT, not MRI.

frontHtml: Identify topiramate as the cause of bilateral angle closure and stop it.
backHtml: bilateral angle closure soon after starting topiramate: stop the drug and use aqueous suppressants and cycloplegics.

frontHtml: Plan retinal screening for a low-risk patient starting hydroxychloroquine.
backHtml: hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye examination, then yearly screening from 5 years (earlier with risk factors).

frontHtml: Stop ethambutol when optic neuropathy develops.
backHtml: visual change on ethambutol means stop the drug now.

frontHtml: Advise patients on tamsulosin before cataract surgery.
backHtml: before cataract surgery, patients taking tamsulosin should tell the surgeon; stopping it is not needed.

frontHtml: Treat acute angle closure precipitated by an antimuscarinic drug.
backHtml: drug-induced pupillary-block angle closure: stop the drug, lower pressure medically, then iridotomy.

frontHtml: Recognize and correct bradycardia caused by topical timolol.
backHtml: consider timolol eye drops as a cause of unexplained bradycardia.

frontHtml: Recognize topical anaesthetic abuse keratopathy and manage it.
backHtml: a non-healing corneal defect in someone using "numbing drops" is anaesthetic toxicity: stop them and refer urgently.

frontHtml: Recognize the visual symptoms of digoxin toxicity and test for it.
backHtml: coloured haloes or yellow vision in a patient on digoxin suggests toxicity: check the level and electrolytes.

frontHtml: Identify nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae as the usual cause of otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome.
backHtml: otitis media plus purulent conjunctivitis suggests beta-lactamase-producing nontypeable H. influenzae .

frontHtml: Explain the anatomic basis for the high incidence of otitis media in young children.
backHtml: eustachian tube anatomy explains why acute otitis media peaks between 6 and 24 months.

frontHtml: Recognize Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the cause of necrotizing otitis externa.
backHtml: necrotizing otitis externa is invasive Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis in older people with diabetes.

frontHtml: Describe the histology of cholesteatoma and distinguish it from cholesterol granuloma.
backHtml: a cholesteatoma is skin (keratin) in the middle ear; it contains no cholesterol.

frontHtml: Identify the geniculate ganglion as the site of viral reactivation in herpes zoster oticus.
backHtml: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of cranial nerve VII.

frontHtml: Relate the anatomy of the mastoid to sigmoid sinus thrombosis as a complication of mastoiditis.
backHtml: mastoid infection can thrombose the adjacent sigmoid sinus and raise intracranial pressure.

frontHtml: Explain why high-dose amoxicillin is used for otitis media in terms of pneumococcal resistance.
backHtml: pneumococci resist penicillins through altered PBPs, which high-dose amoxicillin overcomes.

frontHtml: Identify the cell of origin and histology of vestibular schwannoma.
backHtml: one-sided sensorineural loss plus an internal auditory canal mass is a schwannoma until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Link bilateral vestibular schwannomas to NF2 and the protein merlin.
backHtml: bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the defining feature of NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22).

frontHtml: Predict the cranial nerve findings of an enlarging cerebellopontine angle tumor.
backHtml: a growing cerebellopontine angle tumor affects CN V (corneal reflex) before CN VII weakness becomes obvious.

frontHtml: State the neural crest origin of head and neck paragangliomas.
backHtml: glomus tumors are neural crest-derived paragangliomas; pulsatile tinnitus is the clue.

frontHtml: Associate hereditary paraganglioma with succinate dehydrogenase gene variants.
backHtml: hereditary head and neck paragangliomas usually reflect SDH (complex II) variants.

frontHtml: Associate nasopharyngeal carcinoma with Epstein-Barr virus and one-sided effusion.
