backHtml: an adult with a one-sided middle-ear effusion and a neck node may have EBV-related nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

frontHtml: Connect ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers on the auricle to nucleotide excision repair.
backHtml: ultraviolet damage (pyrimidine dimers) is fixed by nucleotide excision repair; the auricle is a common skin cancer site.

frontHtml: Interpret the Weber and Rinne tests to classify hearing loss.
backHtml: Weber to the bad ear plus a negative Rinne on that ear means conductive loss.

frontHtml: Identify connexin 26 defects as the leading genetic cause of non-syndromic congenital deafness.
backHtml: GJB2 (connexin 26) is the most common genetic cause of non-syndromic congenital hearing loss.

frontHtml: Explain the thyroid defect in Pendred syndrome.
backHtml: hearing loss plus goiter plus an enlarged vestibular aqueduct points to pendrin (Pendred syndrome).

frontHtml: Describe ionic transduction in cochlear hair cells.
backHtml: hair cells depolarize by K + influx from potassium-rich endolymph.

frontHtml: Recognize congenital cytomegalovirus infection as a cause of neonatal hearing loss.
backHtml: congenital CMV is the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural deafness.

frontHtml: Relate the clinical features of Ménière disease to endolymphatic hydrops.
backHtml: Ménière disease = endolymphatic hydrops: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-tone loss, tinnitus, fullness.

frontHtml: Predict the direction of nystagmus in unilateral peripheral vestibular loss.
backHtml: in peripheral vestibular loss, the fast phase of nystagmus beats away from the bad ear.

frontHtml: Distinguish otolith function from semicircular canal function.
backHtml: otolith organs sense linear acceleration and tilt; semicircular canals sense rotation.

frontHtml: Interpret the head impulse test in unilateral vestibular loss.
backHtml: the head impulse test is abnormal (catch-up saccade) when the head is turned towards the damaged side.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of scopolamine-induced angle closure.
backHtml: anticholinergic motion-sickness drugs can precipitate angle-closure glaucoma by causing mydriasis.

frontHtml: Localize vertigo with ipsilateral hearing loss and facial palsy to the AICA territory.
backHtml: vertigo plus sudden one-sided deafness and facial palsy suggests an AICA (lateral pontine) infarct.

frontHtml: Explain the pathogenesis of cauliflower ear after auricular hematoma.
backHtml: cauliflower ear results from undrained blood cutting cartilage off from its perichondrial blood supply.

frontHtml: Distinguish the consequences of otic capsule-sparing and otic capsule-violating temporal bone fractures.
backHtml: otic capsule-violating (transverse) fractures cause sensorineural loss, vertigo and facial palsy.

frontHtml: Select beta-2 transferrin to confirm cerebrospinal fluid leakage.
backHtml: confirm CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea with beta-2 transferrin.

frontHtml: Identify the muscle that opens the eustachian tube and relate it to barotrauma.
backHtml: the tensor veli palatini (CN V3) opens the eustachian tube; a blocked tube causes barotrauma on descent.

frontHtml: Identify the tympanic membrane as the organ most susceptible to primary blast injury.
backHtml: the eardrum is the organ most often injured by a primary blast wave.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of tissue injury from button batteries.
backHtml: button batteries cause rapid alkaline liquefactive necrosis: remove them immediately.

frontHtml: Recognize perilymph fistula as a mechanism of inner-ear barotrauma.
backHtml: sudden sensorineural loss and vertigo after forceful Valsalva suggests a round window perilymph fistula.

frontHtml: Explain mitochondrial susceptibility to aminoglycoside ototoxicity.
backHtml: maternally inherited aminoglycoside deafness = mitochondrial 12S rRNA ( MT-RNR1 ) variant.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of loop diuretic ototoxicity.
backHtml: loop diuretic ototoxicity comes from NKCC1 blockade in the stria vascularis and is usually reversible.

frontHtml: Describe the reversible nature of salicylate ototoxicity.
backHtml: salicylate tinnitus and hearing loss are reversible after stopping the drug.

frontHtml: Recognize the audiometric pattern of cisplatin ototoxicity.
backHtml: cisplatin ototoxicity is bilateral, high-frequency first, sensorineural and usually permanent.

frontHtml: Recognize the clinical findings of bilateral aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity.
backHtml: gentamicin causes bilateral vestibular loss: oscillopsia and imbalance in the dark, not vertigo.

frontHtml: Identify drug combinations that increase ototoxicity.
backHtml: an aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic is the classic synergistic ototoxic combination.

frontHtml: Recognize quinine toxicity (cinchonism) and its hematologic risks.
backHtml: cinchonism (tinnitus, hearing loss, visual blurring) plus thrombocytopenia suggests quinine.

frontHtml: Apply criteria for initial observation versus antibiotics in acute otitis media.
backHtml: non-severe AOM at age 2 or older (or one-sided at 6-23 months) may be observed with a 48-72 hour safety net.

frontHtml: Choose first-line antibiotic therapy for acute otitis media.
backHtml: high-dose amoxicillin is first line for AOM when antibiotics are indicated.

frontHtml: Recognize indications for amoxicillin-clavulanate in acute otitis media.
backHtml: recent amoxicillin use or otitis-conjunctivitis calls for amoxicillin-clavulanate.

frontHtml: Treat necrotizing otitis externa with prolonged systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics.
backHtml: necrotizing otitis externa needs weeks of systemic antipseudomonal therapy, not drops.

frontHtml: Manage uncomplicated acute otitis externa with topical therapy.
backHtml: uncomplicated otitis externa: topical drops, not oral antibiotics.

frontHtml: Evaluate suspected complicated acute mastoiditis with contrast CT.
backHtml: mastoiditis with a fluctuant swelling needs IV antibiotics plus contrast CT to plan drainage.

frontHtml: Refer cholesteatoma for surgical management.
backHtml: cholesteatoma is treated surgically; drops only suppress the discharge.

frontHtml: Manage otitis media with effusion with watchful waiting.
backHtml: post-AOM effusion in a well child is watched for 3 months; no antibiotics, steroids or decongestants.

frontHtml: Treat herpes zoster oticus with combined antiviral and corticosteroid therapy.
backHtml: Ramsay Hunt syndrome: steroid plus antiviral early, and protect the eye.

frontHtml: Order MRI of the internal auditory canals for asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss.
backHtml: asymmetric sensorineural loss or one-sided tinnitus is investigated with gadolinium MRI of the internal auditory canals.

frontHtml: Evaluate unilateral adult middle-ear effusion for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
backHtml: one-sided effusion in an adult: look in the nasopharynx before treating the ear.

frontHtml: Evaluate a suspected middle-ear paraganglioma with imaging rather than biopsy.
backHtml: a red pulsatile retrotympanic mass needs imaging, never biopsy through the drum.

frontHtml: Diagnose NF2-related schwannomatosis from bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
backHtml: bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2-related schwannomatosis.

frontHtml: Select observation for small vestibular schwannomas in appropriate patients.
backHtml: small, stable vestibular schwannomas, especially in older patients, are watched with serial MRI.

frontHtml: Biopsy suspicious auricular skin lesions before treatment.
backHtml: biopsy any non-healing, growing lesion on the auricle before treating it.

frontHtml: Screen paragangliomas for catecholamine secretion before surgery.
backHtml: check metanephrines before operating on any paraganglioma; treat secreting tumors with alpha-blockade first.

frontHtml: Use tuning-fork tests to recognize sudden sensorineural hearing loss.
backHtml: a sudden one-sided loss with Weber to the good ear and a positive Rinne is sensorineural until audiometry says otherwise.

frontHtml: Treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss with early corticosteroids.
backHtml: sudden sensorineural loss: confirm with audiometry and start a corticosteroid early.

frontHtml: Evaluate sudden sensorineural hearing loss for retrocochlear pathology.
backHtml: every sudden sensorineural loss needs a retrocochlear workup, usually MRI of the internal auditory canals.

frontHtml: Manage presbycusis with amplification.
backHtml: presbycusis is treated with hearing aids; it does not need imaging or steroids.

frontHtml: Diagnose otosclerosis from its typical presentation.
backHtml: conductive loss with a normal drum in a young woman suggests otosclerosis.

frontHtml: Follow up a failed newborn hearing screen within the 1-3-6 timeline.
backHtml: a failed newborn hearing screen means diagnostic ABR by 3 months of age.

frontHtml: Manage cerumen impaction as a cause of conductive hearing loss.
backHtml: impacted cerumen causing conductive loss: soften and remove, then recheck hearing.

frontHtml: Recommend prevention for noise-induced hearing loss.
backHtml: noise-induced loss (4 kHz notch) is permanent; prevent progression with hearing protection.

frontHtml: Diagnose Alport syndrome from renal, auditory and ocular findings.
backHtml: hematuria plus sensorineural hearing loss plus lens changes = Alport syndrome (type IV collagen).

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection to protect hearing.
backHtml: symptomatic congenital CMV: 6 months of oral valganciclovir, plus serial hearing tests.

frontHtml: Treat posterior canal BPPV with canalith repositioning.
backHtml: positive Dix-Hallpike: do the Epley maneuver; no imaging or drugs.

frontHtml: Use bedside oculomotor findings to identify central vertigo and order MRI.
backHtml: acute vertigo with a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew = stroke until MRI proves otherwise.

frontHtml: Diagnose vestibular neuritis from bedside findings.
backHtml: vestibular neuritis: continuous vertigo, normal hearing and a peripheral pattern on bedside testing.

frontHtml: Select first-line maintenance therapy for Ménière disease.
backHtml: Ménière maintenance starts with a low-salt diet; suppressants are for attacks only.

frontHtml: Diagnose vestibular migraine.
backHtml: episodic vertigo with migraine features and normal hearing suggests vestibular migraine.

frontHtml: Choose prophylaxis for motion sickness.
backHtml: scopolamine patch before travel is first-line prophylaxis for motion sickness.

frontHtml: Use vestibular rehabilitation for chronic imbalance after vestibular injury.
backHtml: persistent imbalance after vestibular loss: vestibular rehabilitation, and stop suppressants.

frontHtml: Manage auricular hematoma with drainage and compression.
backHtml: auricular hematoma: drain early and compress to prevent cauliflower ear.

frontHtml: Manage an uncomplicated traumatic tympanic membrane perforation.
backHtml: most small traumatic eardrum perforations heal: keep dry, avoid ototoxic drops, follow up.

frontHtml: Manage an aural button battery foreign body as an emergency.
backHtml: a button battery in the ear needs immediate removal, without irrigation.

frontHtml: Manage a live insect in the external ear canal.
backHtml: kill a live insect in the ear with oil or lidocaine before removing it.

frontHtml: Manage traumatic cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea conservatively.
backHtml: traumatic CSF otorrhea: conservative care first, without prophylactic antibiotics.

frontHtml: Use the timing and completeness of traumatic facial palsy to guide management.
backHtml: delayed or incomplete traumatic facial palsy recovers well with conservative care; immediate complete palsy may need surgery.

frontHtml: Manage middle-ear barotrauma.
backHtml: middle-ear barotrauma: symptomatic care and no diving until healed; inner-ear symptoms need urgent evaluation.

frontHtml: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity and change therapy.
backHtml: new ototoxicity on an aminoglycoside: stop it and switch to an effective alternative.

frontHtml: Monitor hearing during prolonged aminoglycoside therapy.
backHtml: get a baseline high-frequency audiogram before prolonged aminoglycoside therapy, then monitor.

frontHtml: Identify an otoprotective strategy for pediatric cisplatin therapy.
backHtml: in children with localized solid tumors, delayed sodium thiosulfate reduces cisplatin hearing loss.

frontHtml: Manage salicylate-induced tinnitus and hearing loss.
backHtml: salicylate ototoxicity is reversible: check the level and reduce the dose.

frontHtml: Avoid aminoglycosides in carriers of mitochondrial ototoxicity susceptibility variants.
backHtml: known MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G carriers should avoid aminoglycosides whenever an alternative exists.

frontHtml: Recognize and manage quinine toxicity.
backHtml: quinine for leg cramps is unsafe; stop it if tinnitus or thrombocytopenia develop.

frontHtml: Reduce the risk of loop diuretic ototoxicity by changing administration.
backHtml: prevent loop diuretic ototoxicity by avoiding rapid high-dose IV pushes, especially in kidney failure.

frontHtml: State the mechanism of VMAT2 inhibitors used for tardive dyskinesia.
backHtml: tardive dyskinesia is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors, which deplete presynaptic dopamine stores.

frontHtml: Explain how NMDA receptor antagonists model the positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
backHtml: NMDA antagonists reproduce the full schizophrenia picture, supporting the glutamate hypothesis.

frontHtml: Recognise clozapine-induced neutropenia and the need to measure the absolute neutrophil count.
backHtml: fever on clozapine means an urgent absolute neutrophil count.

frontHtml: Recall the main structural brain findings in schizophrenia.
backHtml: ventricular enlargement with reduced cortical volume is the classic structural finding in schizophrenia.

frontHtml: Explain why D2 partial agonists do not raise prolactin.
backHtml: D2 partial agonists lower rather than raise prolactin.

frontHtml: Attribute antipsychotic orthostatic hypotension to alpha-1 receptor blockade.
backHtml: orthostatic hypotension from antipsychotics reflects alpha-1 blockade, most with low-potency agents.

frontHtml: Diagnose brief psychotic disorder from its duration and full recovery.
backHtml: psychosis for under a month with full recovery is brief psychotic disorder.

frontHtml: Distinguish schizophreniform disorder from schizophrenia by duration.
backHtml: a schizophrenia-like illness lasting 1 to 6 months is schizophreniform disorder.

frontHtml: Differentiate schizoaffective disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features.
backHtml: psychosis that persists 2 weeks or more without mood symptoms, in an illness dominated by mood episodes, is schizoaffective disorder.

frontHtml: Diagnose delusional disorder.
backHtml: an isolated delusion with intact function is delusional disorder.

frontHtml: Plan the initial evaluation of first-episode psychosis.
backHtml: every first episode of psychosis begins with a drug screen and basic medical tests.

frontHtml: Identify features of psychosis that require neuroimaging.
backHtml: late-onset psychosis with neurological features needs brain imaging first.

frontHtml: Choose clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
backHtml: after two failed adequate antipsychotic trials, use clozapine.

frontHtml: Manage neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
backHtml: in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, stop the drug and give supportive care first.

frontHtml: Manage metabolic adverse effects of second-generation antipsychotics.
backHtml: antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is managed by switching to a metabolically lighter drug and lifestyle measures.

frontHtml: Use long-acting injectable antipsychotics for relapse due to non-adherence.
backHtml: relapse from non-adherence is an indication for a long-acting injectable antipsychotic.

frontHtml: Treat antipsychotic-induced akathisia.
backHtml: akathisia responds to dose reduction or propranolol rather than anticholinergics.

frontHtml: Recognise and manage clozapine-induced myocarditis.
backHtml: fever, tachycardia and a raised troponin early in clozapine treatment mean myocarditis: stop the drug.

frontHtml: Treat tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor.
backHtml: treat bothersome tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor.

frontHtml: Treat catatonia with benzodiazepines.
backHtml: treat catatonia with lorazepam, then ECT if needed.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor.
backHtml: benzodiazepines raise the frequency of GABA-A channel opening; barbiturates raise its duration.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism and risks of flumazenil.
backHtml: flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site but risks seizures in dependent patients.

frontHtml: State the mechanism and features of buspirone.
backHtml: buspirone is a non-sedating, non-addictive 5-HT1A partial agonist with a delayed onset.

frontHtml: Explain the physiology of paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm in hyperventilation.
backHtml: hyperventilation lowers ionised calcium through alkalosis, causing tingling and carpopedal spasm.

frontHtml: Identify the amygdala as the core structure for conditioned fear.
backHtml: the amygdala acquires conditioned fear; exposure therapy builds prefrontal extinction learning.

frontHtml: Recall the neural circuit implicated in OCD.
backHtml: OCD is linked to overactive orbitofrontal-caudate-thalamic circuits.

frontHtml: Explain the use of beta-blockers in performance anxiety.
backHtml: propranolol relieves the peripheral adrenergic symptoms of performance anxiety.

frontHtml: Identify clomipramine as the tricyclic effective in OCD.
backHtml: clomipramine is the serotonergic tricyclic used for OCD.

frontHtml: Choose first-line pharmacotherapy for generalized anxiety disorder.
backHtml: start an SSRI or SNRI for generalized anxiety disorder.

frontHtml: Treat panic disorder with an SSRI and CBT.
backHtml: panic disorder is treated with an SSRI and/or CBT, not long-term benzodiazepines.

frontHtml: Exclude medical emergencies before attributing chest symptoms to panic.
backHtml: exclude cardiac causes before diagnosing a panic attack in someone at cardiovascular risk.

frontHtml: Treat a specific phobia with exposure therapy.
backHtml: specific phobia is treated with exposure therapy.

frontHtml: Diagnose agoraphobia.
backHtml: fear of several situations where escape would be hard is agoraphobia.

frontHtml: Manage performance-only social anxiety.
backHtml: use as-needed propranolol for performance-only anxiety.

frontHtml: Select exposure and response prevention for OCD.
backHtml: the psychotherapy of choice for OCD is exposure and response prevention.

frontHtml: Recognise body dysmorphic disorder and avoid cosmetic intervention.
backHtml: body dysmorphic disorder needs CBT and an SSRI, not cosmetic surgery.

frontHtml: Choose first-line treatment for PTSD.
backHtml: trauma-focused psychotherapy is first-line for PTSD; avoid benzodiazepines.

frontHtml: Distinguish acute stress disorder from PTSD by timing.
backHtml: the same trauma-response picture is acute stress disorder before 1 month and PTSD after.

frontHtml: Diagnose adjustment disorder.
backHtml: distress after a stressor that falls short of other disorders is adjustment disorder.

frontHtml: Diagnose separation anxiety disorder in a child.
backHtml: school refusal driven by fear for a parent's safety is separation anxiety disorder.

frontHtml: Plan a benzodiazepine taper in an older adult.
backHtml: taper long-term benzodiazepines slowly, especially in older adults.

frontHtml: Treat trichotillomania with habit reversal training.
backHtml: trichotillomania is treated with habit reversal training.

frontHtml: Identify medical causes of anxiety symptoms.
backHtml: look for hyperthyroidism and arrhythmia before diagnosing an anxiety disorder.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism and treatment of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
backHtml: amiloride blocks lithium entry through ENaC and treats lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

frontHtml: Explain the thiazide-lithium interaction.
backHtml: thiazides raise lithium by increasing proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption.

frontHtml: Explain the tyramine reaction with MAO inhibitors.
backHtml: MAO inhibitors plus tyramine release noradrenaline and cause a hypertensive crisis.

frontHtml: Recall the seizure risk of bupropion and its contraindications.
backHtml: avoid bupropion in eating disorders because of seizure risk.

frontHtml: State the mechanism and clinical niche of mirtazapine.
